blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper by Delgado et al. that tackles the challenge of person-name disambiguation on the web, where multiple individuals share the same name. The author highlights the problem of search engines returning mixed results for namesakes, making it difficult to find information about a specific person. The paper presents an unsupervised algorithm that clusters web pages based on the individuals they refer to, without requiring prior training. The algorithm uses n-grams (specifically 3-grams) of capitalized words from web pages, weighted by z-scores to measure similarity between pages. The cosine distance is then applied to determine if pages belong to the same cluster, with a threshold function accounting for shared n-grams and page sizes. The algorithm performs competitively with the best entrants in the WePS-1, WePS-2, and WePS-3 competitions, achieving high precision and recall. The key insight is the use of unsupervised n-gram-based similarity with statistical weighting to effectively disambiguate person names in web search results.
paper_title: An unsupervised algorithm for person-name disambiguation on the web
paper_abstract: This paper presents an unsupervised approach for the task of clustering the results of a search engine when the query is a person name shared by different individuals. We propose an algorithm that calculates the number of clusters and establishes the groups of web pages according to the different individuals without the need to any training data or predefined thresholds, as the successful state of the art systems do. In addition, most of those systems do not deal with social media web pages and their performance could fail in a real scenario. In this paper we also propose a heuristic method for the treatment of social networking profiles. Our approach is compared with four gold standard collections for this task obtaining really competitive results, comparable to those obtained by some approaches with supervision.
